CONGRANT.TITLE: 2024 Texas Prefreshman Engineering Program (TexPrep) Engineering Ambassadors
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The Engineering Ambassadors program sponsored by the Halliburton Foundation enables the recruitment of top engineering students as summer mentors for TexPREP. Dr. Jesus Gonzalez (PI) is an Assistant Professor of Practice of Mechanical Engineering and Engineering Technology and TexPREP Director at UTRGV, which provides 600 top middle/high school students a challenging seven-week academic program that prepares them for careers in STEM. TexPREP goals are to increase the number of students from underrepresented groups (over 40% female, 95% Hispanic and 65% low-income) entering STEM fields; reinforce students’ math preparation; increase college retention; and acquaint students with STEM careers. Ambassadors (engineering and STEM undergrads expressing interest in oil & gas and 3.0+ GPA) gain valuable leadership experience assisting TexPREP participants with courses and engineering projects throughout the summer program and act as excellent role models for them. Ambassadors participate in a 2-day engineering lab experience with the UTCRS directed by Dr. Tarawneh, attend a virtual meeting with a Halliburton representative to explore employment opportunities, and are encouraged to take a course offered by Dr. Pournik (Petrophysics, drilling and completion, reservoir and production, and natural gas engineering). These opportunities will shape their career paths and give the Ambassadors a rich experience to share with TexPREP students.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Brownsville UTRGV Texas Prefreshman Engineering Program (TexPREP)
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The Texas Prefreshman Engineering Program (TexPREP) is an intensive four-year program providing middle and high school students with the opportunity to prepare for and learn about promising careers through a seven-week summer curriculum and a series of follow up monthly meetings during the academic year. TexPREP at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) in Brownsville, Texas, enables many students from throughout the fast-growing South Texas region to prepare and become the first generation in their families to benefit from post-secondary education in STEM fields and contribute to the economic vitality of our communities.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Research: Writing Assignment Tutor Training in STEM, an Interdisciplinary Approach to Enhance Student Writing in STEM
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Writing Assignment Tutor Training in STEM (WATTS), an Interdisciplinary Approach for the Enhancement of Student Writing in STEM fields
PROJECT DESCRIPTION
Overview and Knowledge Base
Undergraduate STEM writing skills, especially in engineering fields, need improvement1. Research has shown that students in STEM fields lack strong writing skills2. Although STEM students learn writing skills in first-year composition (FYC) courses, they often fail to transfer them to discipline-specific writing, mainly due to a perception that English courses are subjective and unrelated to their majors3. However, they view their major courses as fact-based and objective4,5. Therefore, writing skills that should continue to be developed throughout their undergraduate disciplines may remain stagnant.Despite the importance of discipline-specific writing skills, many instructors remain resistant to incorporating writing into their courses6. Engineering instructors report this resistance primarily due to large enrollments, lack of time, or poor quality of student writing7. In a recent study of engineering instructors, 60% perceived teaching assistants (graduate or undergraduate) trained to support writing to be the most valuable in helping them to include more writing in their courses7.Institutional efforts in STEM programs are often focused on retention, which justifiably impacts the approach to curricula, instruction, and funding for research efforts on and implementation of student interventions. In addition, given the cost of higher education, public pressure on institutions to graduate students within four years has increased, leading to programs that are intensive in the development of disciplinary competencies, with writing skills unintentionally becoming a secondary concern.To address these challenges, this application proposes to expand the implementation of the innovative and cost-effect Writing Assignment Tutor Training in STEM (WATTS) process which is focused on training generalist tutors to help students write better in the students’ own disciplinary genre. It also proposes to systematically evaluate its impact on outcomes related to students (and student writing), peer tutors, engineering instructors, writing centers, and writing tutor supervisors. While the current project research is being conducted in both engineering and engineering technology courses, the future goal is to expand it to other STEM fields. WATTS is founded on knowledge transfer theory and employs the frameworks of writing in the discipline (WID) and genre theory8,9,3. The collaborations between engineering instructors and writing centers enable instructors to provide WID support in their courses without adding substantially to their workloads; WATTS also has the potential to mitigate student misconceptions about writing and potentially produce better short- and long-term writing skill outcomes. The requirement to communicate with peers outside of engineering provides students with a learning opportunity that extends past basic writing skills and promotes WID10. The results of our preliminary research on WATTS have motivated the formulation of this proposal’s Specific Aims:Specific Aim 1: Determine the impact of WATTS on student- and tutor-level outcomes. Identify mitigating and moderating effects of WATTS using data from students and tutors.• Objective 1.1: Identify the effects of WATTS on student perceptions and likelihood to use tutoring.• Objective 1.2: Identify the effects of WATTS on student writing.• Objective 1.3: Identify the effects of WATTS on tutors’ self-efficacy and tutoring practices.Specific Aim 2: Determine the impact of WATTS on instructors and on writing center outcomes to enhance the implementation, training, and development of WATTS.• Objective 2.1: Identify instructor attributes that contribute to successful WATTS implementation.• Objective 2.2: Identify writing center attributes that contribute to successful WATTS implementation.• Objective 2.3: Identify elements of joint training of instructor and tutor supervisor that contribute to WATTS successful implementation.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Enhancing Engineering and Technology Career Pathways: Recruiting, Retaining, and Graduating Underrepresented Students in the Era of Digital Transformation
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), a major Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI)
located in the border region of United States and Mexico is seeking to increase participation, retention
and graduation rates among minority low-income students in the critically needed engineering and
technology programs. This project provides innovative ways for adapting effective evidence based
curricular and co-curricular activities aimed to improve undergraduate student academic success. The
primary goal of this project is to encourage and increase the number of students towards obtaining their
degrees in STEM by providing 30 undergradaute students with four-year scholarships, and 17
undergraduate students with two-year scholarships (47 total), spread across four cohorts. In addition, we
emphasize on improved student technical workforce readiness levels by establishing an academic support
system at the College of Engineering and Computer Science (COECS) to encourage students to pursue
careers in emerging fields of engineering and technology.
Building on existing student support services at UTRGV, this project includes technical and academic
success workshops, professional development, peer mentoring, industry certifications and internships, and
developing course modules integrated with Engineering Technology and Manufacturing Engineering
curriculum. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include: (a) To increase student
enrollment of Manufacturing and Engineering Technology undergraduate programs created to train and
prepare students with high-tech skills in the fields of manufacturing, automation and systems engineering;
(b) Developing an Eco-System in COECS with tailored student centric activities to address student’s precollege
experience, social-cultural experience, institutional experience, and college experience
specifically targeting underrepresented demographics; (c) Financially support undergraduate students by
awarding S-STEM scholarships over the grant period; and (d) Build partnerships with industry to provide
more learning and internship opportunities for students.

Embedded Curriculum with Industry-recognized Certifications to Improve the Marketability of Engineering Technology Graduates
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Embedded Curriculum with Industry Recognized Certifications to Improve the Marketability of Engineering Technology Graduates
The Fourth Industrial Revolution is challenging the industries to change the way they manage and operate the manufacturing environment. This leads to the transformation of the world through artificial intelligence, next-generation robotics, automation, big data analytics, 5G technology and Internet of Things. This idea of Industry 4.0 forces the change in the industries of today and tomorrow. In this, cyber physical systems communicate with one another using the Internet of Things. The manufacturing sector takes full advantage of these technologies to produce innovative products to enhance the human experience. Contrary to the prediction of huge job loss due to these new technologies, more jobs are being created at a rapid pace. This is evident in the number of job openings growing at double-digit rates since mid-2017. This trend created a new set of problems in finding a matching workforce that will support the growing areas of advanced manufacturing in digital talent, skilled production and operational managers. The digital talent includes programming and managing a pool of computer-enabled machines and equipment.
This demands for qualified workers in key areas of technical trades. This includes technologies such as, Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), Computer Numerical Control, Coordinate Metrology, Industrial Robots, Mobile Autonomous Robots, Collaborative Robots and Automation. In the Recent Polls of American Distribution & Logistics Companies, 50% say that they see a critical need for these technologies to garner technology driven operational efficiencies.
According to the study by Deloitte and the Manufacturing Institute, the skills needed in the above areas may leave an estimated 2.4 million positions unfilled between 2018 and 2028, with a potential economic impact of $ 2.5 trillion. Further, the study shows that the positions relating to digital talent, skilled production, and operational managers may be three times as difficult to fill in the next three years.
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley has undertaken an initiative to address the growing needs of skilled human power in these critical areas that are very important for the local industries to sustain the competitive edge in the global manufacturing environment. Industries often look for graduates that are ready to be employed with minimum on the job training. The certifications offered by the professional institutions serve as the enabling tool for industries to assess the potential of newly minted graduate who have minimum field experience.
This paper presents the details on the innovative development of the embedded engineering technology curriculum with industry recognized certifications in the much-needed areas of Industry 4.0. This will invariably help the industries to mitigate the difficult-to-fill workforce needs in the critical areas of advanced manufacturing. Also, discussed in detail in the paper are the pedagogical aspects of the Engineering Technology curriculum and the seamless integration of industry recognized certifications that have the potential to enhance the marketability of its graduates.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Solar Energy Certificate for Engineering Technology Students
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Solar Energy is the fastest-growing energy resource in the United States and the world. This industry just hit an important milestone in 2019 of completing two million solar systems installations in the country and is expected to duplicate this quantity by 2023.
Organizations and home and business owners in our South Texas region are starting to recognize the benefits of this type of renewable energy. And with the drop in the cost of the components and installation of the solar system, the future for this industry seems promising.
Our Program of Engineering Technology, which is part of the College of Engineering and Computer Science of the University of XXXX, is committed to providing our students with the set of skills that make them successful in their careers, but overall, professionals that can contribute to the sustainable development of our region.
In this paper, the authors present the scheme for a new certificate in Solar Energy Systems as a part of the Engineering Technology curriculum. This proposal is supported by our departmental Vision of giving the students a robust technical knowledge through industry certificates along with the degree courses, so they can be industry-ready and able to deliver results as soon as they join the workforce, or as entrepreneurs. The backbone of this proposal lays not only in our existing courses in renewable energies and specifically solar energy systems, but also in the expertise of our faculty, and the relationship of the department with the local industry in this field.
The solar systems installations by themselves, are endeavors that require an understanding of different fields, such a mechanical, electrical, power electronics, photovoltaics, and management. An important characteristic of the proposed certificate is the holistic approach in which we will be preparing the students not only with the technical skills and the specifics of this technology, but also with all the processes associated with this industry; such as local and federal regulations, codes, grants and tax incentives, and the requirements to connect to the grid of the utility companies.
This project represents an important effort within our department, and we believe it has an important content of innovation in engineering education that we would like to share with the ASEE community.

SERVICE_COLLEGE.ORG: Reviewing and Restructuring the Brownsville Signature Programs into a new Department
SERVICE_COLLEGE.DESC: The charge of this committee is to review all information and technology programs and consider restructuring into a new department to be housed on the Brownsville campus.
SERVICE_COLLEGE.ACCOMPLISH: The name and a structure for the new Brownsville department• The prospect of initiating a BS in IT to complement the existing MS in IT (and considering any alignments and/or conflicts with the COBE BS in CIS)• Any needed curriculum alignments and/or changes including the prefixes for the IT and Cybersecurity courses keeping in mind that the programs/curriculum offered by the new department can include courses offered by other departments including Computer Science, and vice versa; i.e. the other departments can use courses offered by the new department. This is important in order to keep the SCH credit in the department from which the course is offered.• The faculty strengths and needs on the Brownsville campus to support the programs within the proposed department.• Alignment with existing departments and mainly Computer Science which may eventually become an Edinburg signature program with IT (and cybersecurity) becoming Brownsville signature program(s).
